{{Short description|3-Dimensional analogue of a pendulum}}
[[File:Spherical pendulum Lagrangian mechanics.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Spherical pendulum: angles and velocities.]]

In [[physics]], a '''spherical pendulum''' is a higher dimensional analogue of the [[pendulum]]. It consists of a [[mass]] {{mvar|m}} moving without [[friction]] on the surface of a [[sphere]]. The only [[force]]s acting on the mass are the [[reaction (physics)|reaction]] from the sphere and [[gravity]].

It is convenient to use the [[spherical coordinates]] to describe the position of the mass in terms of {{nowrap|<math>(r, \theta, \phi)</math>}}, where {{mvar|r}} is fixed such that <math>r = l</math>.

==Lagrangian mechanics==

{{main|Lagrangian mechanics}}

Routinely, in order to write down the kinetic <math>T=\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2</math> and potential <math>V</math> parts of the Lagrangian <math>L=T-V</math> in arbitrary [[generalized coordinates]] the position of the mass is expressed along Cartesian axes. Here, following the conventions shown in the diagram,
:<math>x=l\sin\theta\cos\phi</math>
:<math>y=l\sin\theta\sin\phi</math>
:<math>z=l(1-\cos\theta)</math>.
Next, time derivatives of these coordinates are taken, to obtain velocities along the axes
:<math>\dot x=l\cos\theta\cos\phi\,\dot\theta-l\sin\theta\sin\phi\,\dot\phi</math>
:<math>\dot y=l\cos\theta\sin\phi\,\dot\theta+l\sin\theta\cos\phi\,\dot\phi</math>
:<math>\dot z=l\sin\theta\,\dot\theta</math>.
Thus,

:<math>
v^2=\dot x ^2+\dot y ^2+\dot z ^2
=l^2\left(\dot\theta ^2+\sin^2\theta\,\dot\phi ^2\right)
</math>

and

:<math>
T=\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2
=\tfrac{1}{2}ml^2\left(\dot\theta ^2+\sin^2\theta\,\dot\phi ^2\right)
</math>
:<math>
V=mg\,z=mg\,l(1-\cos\theta)
</math>

The Lagrangian, with constant parts removed, is<ref name=":0">{{cite book|last=Landau|first=Lev Davidovich|title=Course of Theoretical Physics: Volume 1 Mechanics|author2=Evgenii Mikhailovich Lifshitz|publisher=Butterworth-Heinenann|year=1976|isbn=0750628960|pages=33–34}}</ref> 

:<math>
L=\frac{1}{2}
ml^2\left(
  \dot{\theta}^2+\sin^2\theta\ \dot{\phi}^2
\right)
+ mgl\cos\theta.
</math>

The [[Euler–Lagrange equations|Euler–Lagrange equation]] involving the polar angle <math>\theta</math>

:<math>
\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial}{\partial\dot\theta}L-\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}L=0
</math>
gives
:<math>
\frac{d}{dt}
\left(ml^2\dot{\theta}
\right)
-ml^2\sin\theta\cdot\cos\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2+
mgl\sin\theta =0
</math>
and
:<math>
\ddot\theta=\sin\theta\cos\theta\dot\phi ^2-\frac{g}{l}\sin\theta
</math>
When <math>\dot\phi=0</math> the equation reduces to the [[differential equation]] for the motion of a [[Pendulum (mathematics)|simple gravity pendulum]].

Similarly, the Euler–Lagrange equation involving the azimuth <math>\phi</math>,

:<math>
\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial}{\partial\dot\phi}L-\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}L=0
</math>
gives
:<math>
\frac{d}{dt}
\left(
  ml^2\sin^2\theta
  \cdot 
  \dot{\phi}
\right)
=0
</math>.
The last equation shows that [[angular momentum]] around the vertical axis, <math>|\mathbf L_z| = l\sin\theta \times ml\sin\theta\,\dot\phi</math>  is conserved. The factor <math>ml^2\sin^2\theta</math> will play a role in the Hamiltonian formulation below.

The second order differential equation determining the evolution of <math>\phi</math> is thus
:<math>\ddot\phi\,\sin\theta = -2\,\dot\theta\,\dot{\phi}\,\cos\theta</math>.

The azimuth <math>\phi</math>, being absent from the Lagrangian, is a [[cyclic coordinate]], which implies that its [[conjugate momentum]] is a [[constant of motion]].

The [[conical pendulum]] refers to the special solutions where <math>\dot\theta=0</math> and <math>\dot\phi</math> is a constant not depending on time.

==Hamiltonian mechanics==
{{main|Hamiltonian mechanics}}

The Hamiltonian is

:<math>H=P_\theta\dot \theta + P_\phi\dot \phi-L</math>

where conjugate momenta are

:<math>P_\theta=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \theta}=ml^2\cdot \dot \theta</math>

and

:<math>P_\phi=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \phi} = ml^2 \sin^2\! \theta \cdot \dot \phi</math>.

In terms of coordinates and momenta it reads

<math display="block">H = \underbrace{\left[\frac{1}{2}ml^2\dot\theta^2 + \frac{1}{2}ml^2\sin^2\theta\dot \phi^2\right]}_{T} + \underbrace{ \bigg[-mgl\cos\theta\bigg]}_{V}=
{P_\theta^2\over 2ml^2}+{P_\phi^2\over 2ml^2\sin^2\theta}-mgl\cos\theta</math>

Hamilton's equations will give [[time evolution]] of coordinates and momenta in four first-order differential equations

:<math>\dot {\theta}={P_\theta \over ml^2}</math>
:<math>\dot {\phi}={P_\phi \over ml^2\sin^2\theta}</math>
:<math>\dot {P_\theta}={P_\phi^2\over ml^2\sin^3\theta}\cos\theta-mgl\sin\theta</math>
:<math>\dot {P_\phi}=0</math>

Momentum <math>P_\phi</math> is a constant of motion. That is a consequence of the [[rotational symmetry]] of the system around the vertical axis.{{dubious|reason=The system is not symmetrical, rather it is rotation-invariant in the sense that its behaviour does not depend on the rotation around the vertical axis.|date=October 2021}}

== Trajectory ==
[[File:SphaerischesPendelAnima.gif|thumb|250x250px|Trajectory of a spherical pendulum.]]
Trajectory of the mass on the sphere can be obtained from the expression for the total energy

:<math>E=\underbrace{\left[\frac{1}{2}ml^2\dot\theta^2 + \frac{1}{2}ml^2\sin^2\theta \dot \phi^2\right]}_{T}+\underbrace{ \bigg[-mgl\cos\theta\bigg]}_{V}</math>

by noting that the vertical component of angular momentum <math>L_z = ml^2\sin^2\!\theta \,\dot\phi</math> is a constant of motion, independent of time.<ref name=":0" /> This is true because neither gravity nor the reaction from the sphere act in directions that would affect this component of angular momentum.

Hence

:<math>E=\frac{1}{2}ml^2\dot\theta^2 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{L_z^2}{ml^2\sin^2\theta}-mgl\cos\theta</math>
:<math>\left(\frac{d\theta}{dt}\right)^2=\frac{2}{ml^2}\left[E-\frac{1}{2}\frac{L_z^2}{ml^2\sin^2\theta}+mgl\cos\theta\right]</math>

which leads to an [[elliptic integral]] of the first kind<ref name=":0" /> for <math>\theta</math>

:<math>t(\theta)=\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}ml^2}\int\left[E-\frac{1}{2}\frac{L_z^2}{ml^2\sin^2\theta}+mgl\cos\theta\right]^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,d\theta</math>

and an elliptic integral of the third kind for <math>\phi</math>

:<math>\phi(\theta)=\frac{L_z}{l\sqrt{2m}}\int\sin^{-2}\theta \left[E-\frac{1}{2}\frac{L_z^2}{ml^2\sin^2\theta}+mgl\cos\theta\right]^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,d\theta</math>.

The angle <math>\theta</math> lies between two circles of latitude,<ref name=":0" /> where

:<math>E>\frac{1}{2}\frac{L_z^2}{ml^2\sin^2\theta}-mgl\cos\theta</math>.
